1065.title: The tannaim
1065.hook: the sages of the Mishnah, from Hillel's time to Rabbi Judah the Prince
1065.howItsDone: When Jews study the Mishnah they quote it by its teachers, saying 'Rabbi Meir says' or 'the sages say', and it is a custom to repeat a teaching in the name of the one who said it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why it was written down: a terse text, made to go back into the mouth. Your line: write it before it's lost. Today, the people whose words were saved.

Open the Mishnah almost anywhere and you hear a room full of people. Rabbi Meir says this. Rabbi Judah says that. Rabbi Shimon disagrees, and the sages say something else. The house of Shammai, the house of Hillel. Rabban Gamaliel, Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Eliezer. It reads less like a rulebook than the minutes of a very long meeting, with everyone's name attached to what they said. The Talmud has a single word for each of these teachers, and it's today's word.
screen: `RABBI MEIR SAYS. RABBI JUDAH SAYS.` → `A ROOM FULL OF NAMES.` → `ONE WORD FOR EACH OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Tanna. In the plural, tannaim. It's an Aramaic word, and Jastrow's dictionary of Talmudic Aramaic ties it to repeating, and so to teaching, because this teaching was learned by saying it over and over. The tannaim are the sages of the Mishnah, from Hillel and Shammai down to Rabbi Judah the Prince, who gathered their words. Hillel, patient. Shammai, strict. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, who rebuilt after the Temple fell. Rabbi Akiva. And Rabbi Meir, a name the Talmud reads as one who gives light. In tractate Eruvin it says that wasn't even his given name: he was called Meir because he lit up the eyes of the sages in the law. Now a surprise. In tractate Sanhedrin, the Talmud says a teaching in the Mishnah with no name on it follows Rabbi Meir, and adds: all of them follow Rabbi Akiva, his teacher. Even the unsigned lines have a teacher behind them, and a teacher behind him. A second surprise: the same word, tanna, also names a reciter in the house of study who had memorized great stores of teachings and could repeat them on request. And the Talmud, in tractate Sotah, teases them, in paraphrase: the tanna recites and doesn't know what he's saying. Repeating isn't understanding. The tannaim gave the teaching its words. Someone still had to explain them.
screen: `TANNA: ONE WHO REPEATS, AND TEACHES.` · `HILLEL TO RABBI JUDAH THE PRINCE.` · `MEIR: HE LIT UP THE SAGES' EYES.` · `UNSIGNED LINES STILL HAVE A TEACHER.` · then, large: `THE TEACHERS OF THE MISHNAH.`

segments.voice: Breathe in on Rabbi and out on Meir, the one who gave light, and let the name settle the way a tanna settled a teaching, by repeating it until it's yours. Then bring to mind someone who lit up a subject for you: a teacher, a parent, a coworker who explained what nobody else could. If you pray, you can give thanks for them.

1066.title: The amoraim
1066.hook: the sages of the Gemara, who discussed the Mishnah for three centuries
1066.howItsDone: Talmud study is traditionally done in pairs, a chavruta, where two learners read aloud, question each other and argue their way to the meaning of a passage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tanna, a teacher of the Mishnah, and Rabbi Meir, who lit up the sages' eyes. Your line: the teachers of the mishnah. Today, the ones who explained them.

A sage is bathing in the Jordan River. A rough stranger sees him from the bank and, in one leap, jumps into the water after him. The sage is Rabbi Yochanan. The stranger is a man the Talmud calls Resh Lakish, and the story says he had been living as a robber. Rabbi Yochanan says: your strength should be for Torah. Resh Lakish answers: your beauty should be for women. They strike a deal: if he'll turn to study, Rabbi Yochanan will give him his sister in marriage. He does. And the robber becomes a sage whose words fill the Talmud.
screen: `A LEAP INTO THE JORDAN.` → `YOUR STRENGTH FOR TORAH.` → `THE ROBBER BECOMES A SAGE.`

segments.voice: Amora. In the plural, amoraim. The tannaim gave the Mishnah its words. The amoraim are the sages who came after, in the land of Israel and in Babylonia, and spent generations discussing those words line by line. Their discussion is the Gemara. Mishnah plus Gemara: the Talmud. The word is Aramaic, and Jastrow's dictionary ties it to the verb to say: a speaker, an expounder. A few pairs to know: Rav and Shmuel in Babylonia, Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish in the land of Israel, and later Abaye and Rava. They're remembered in pairs. Explaining was done with someone. Back to the riverbank, in tractate Bava Metzia. Years later, after a bitter quarrel, Resh Lakish dies, and Rabbi Yochanan is crushed. The sages send him a brilliant student, Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat. Whatever Rabbi Yochanan says, Rabbi Elazar answers: there's a teaching that supports you. Rabbi Yochanan can't bear it. In paraphrase: are you like the son of Lakish? When I said something, he raised twenty-four objections, I gave twenty-four answers, and the matter came clear on its own. You only tell me I'm right. I know I'm right. The story ends in grief, with Rabbi Yochanan crying out for his friend. For the amoraim, explaining wasn't agreeing. It was pushing back, hard, until the teaching came clear.
screen: `AFTER THE TANNAIM, THE AMORAIM.` · `AMORA: ONE WHO SAYS, WHO EXPOUNDS.` · `RAV AND SHMUEL; ABAYE AND RAVA.` · `TWENTY-FOUR OBJECTIONS, AND IT CAME CLEAR.` · then, large: `THE EXPLAINERS.`

segments.voice: Say the name Resh Lakish quietly a few times, the man who leapt into the river, until it stays. Then bring to mind someone who pushes back on you in a way that leaves you clearer instead of smaller, and hold their face for a while. If you pray, you can give thanks for them; if not, just notice what they've given you.

1067.title: Six orders
1067.hook: the Mishnah has six orders; Shas is their abbreviation
1067.howItsDone: Students learn the six orders by name, and when a person or a study group completes a tractate or the whole of Shas, they hold a siyum, a festive meal, and recite the hadran, which promises to return to what was learned.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the amora, and Resh Lakish with his twenty-four objections. Your line: the explainers. Today, the map of everything they explained.

On a shelf in a house of study stands a long row of matching volumes, tall and heavy, with gold letters on the spines. Someone points at the whole row and calls it by one short word: Shas. You hear it elsewhere too. A person who knows Shas. A celebration for finishing Shas. It sounds like a nickname, and in a way it is: two Hebrew letters, shin and samekh, standing in for two words. Those two words are a map of the whole Mishnah.
screen: `A LONG ROW OF HEAVY VOLUMES.` → `ONE SHORT WORD: SHAS.` → `TWO LETTERS, TWO WORDS.`

segments.voice: Shas. Shin for shishah, six. Samekh for sedarim, orders. Six orders. The Mishnah, and the Talmud built on it, is arranged in six large sections, and Shas became a name for the whole thing. Here they are. Zeraim, seeds: blessings and farming. Moed, appointed time: Shabbat, festivals and fasts. Nashim, women: marriage, divorce and vows. Nezikin, damages: courts, property, harm, and the sayings of the fathers. Kodashim, holy things: the Temple's offerings. Tohorot, purities: what makes a person or a thing pure or impure. Students hold the list with a traditional trick: the first letters spell two little Hebrew words, z'man nakat, roughly, he took time. Now hear the list as a whole. It starts in a field, with food. Then the calendar, the weeks and the seasons. Then the home, between two people. Then out to the neighbors, the market and the court. Then up to the Temple. And finally the body, the house, and what is pure. Some readers hear a map of a whole life: what you eat, when you rest, whom you love, how you treat the person next door, how you come near to God. Nothing is left out as too ordinary. A wedding, a pothole and a holy day sit on the same shelf, under one short word. That's the claim hidden in the abbreviation: it all belongs to one Torah.
screen: `SHIN, SAMEKH: SHISHAH SEDARIM.` · `SEEDS, TIME, WOMEN.` · `DAMAGES, HOLY THINGS, PURITIES.` · `A FIELD, A CALENDAR, A HOME, A COURT.` · then, large: `SIX ORDERS.`

segments.voice: On each out-breath, say one name quietly: Zeraim, Moed, Nashim, Nezikin, Kodashim, Tohorot. Go round again, slower, and let each name bring up one part of your own life: a meal, your calendar, someone you love, a neighbor, a quiet moment, your own body. Keep circling, gently, until the time is up.

1068.title: Seeds
1068.hook: the first order covers blessings and farming
1068.howItsDone: Jews say a blessing before eating, with different endings for bread, fruit of the tree, fruit of the ground and other foods; in the land of Israel, farmers who keep these laws still set aside tithes and observe the seventh year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shas, the six orders: Zeraim, Moed, Nashim, Nezikin, Kodashim, Tohorot. Your line: six orders. Today, into the first one.

A farmer walks out at dawn to a field of wheat that's ready. Before a single stalk is cut, a list of questions is waiting for her. Which edge of the field stays standing? What happens to the stalks she drops? Did she plant two kinds of seed in one row? Is this the year the land is supposed to rest? Which part goes to someone else? On a grocery receipt, a harvest looks simple. The Mishnah's first order sees a web of obligations, and it's named for what goes into the ground.
screen: `A FIELD AT DAWN, READY TO CUT.` → `A LIST OF QUESTIONS WAITING.` → `NAMED FOR WHAT GOES IN THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Zeraim. Seeds. The first of the six orders opens with blessings, which is tomorrow's story, then goes out to the farm and stays there. Walk a growing season with it. Before planting, there's Kilayim, mixed kinds. The Torah says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "thou shalt not sow thy field with two kinds of seed." So the Mishnah asks the practical questions: how far apart must two crops be? What counts as two kinds? Then Sheviit, the seventh year. The Torah tells the farmer to let the land rest, and says the poor may eat what grows on its own. Then the harvest, and here the gifts begin. Peah, the corner of the field, left for the poor. Terumot and Maaserot, the portions set aside for the priests and the Levites, who had no fields of their own. And at the end of the order, Bikkurim, the first fruits brought up to the Temple. Notice the pattern. At every stage, the harvest is never only the farmer's. Something goes to the poor, something to the priest and the Levite, something to the land itself, which gets its rest, and something back to God. Jewish law ties these farm laws largely to the land of Israel, so a Jewish farmer in Ohio isn't bound by most of them. But the order still speaks to anyone who eats: food arrives already carrying other people's shares.
screen: `ZERAIM: THE FIRST ORDER, SEEDS.` · `MIXED KINDS AND THE SEVENTH YEAR.` · `THE CORNER, THE TITHES, FIRST FRUITS.` · `A HARVEST IS NEVER ONLY YOURS.` · then, large: `SEEDS.`

segments.voice: Hold something small you're about to eat, an apple, a piece of bread, and trace it backward: who picked it, packed it, drove it, what field it grew in, what rain fell on it. 1069.title: Why blessings come first
1069.hook: a book about farming opens with blessings: thank before you take
1069.tomorrow: The corner of the field (Mishnah Peah)
1069.howItsDone: Jews say a blessing before eating and another after, and there are blessings for seeing lightning, mountains or the sea, for good news and for bad; the rules for all of them are set out in tractate Berakhot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zeraim, seeds: a harvest that carries other people's shares. Your line: seeds. Today, page one of that order.

What should the first page of a farming law book talk about? Soil, maybe. When to plant. How deep. The Mishnah's order of seeds does get to fields and furrows. But before anyone talks about corners or tithes or the seventh year, it opens with a book called Berakhot. Blessings. Prayer at night and in the morning. Words to say before you bite into bread. A farming book that starts with thank you. Today, why.
screen: `A FARMING BOOK. PAGE ONE?` → `NOT SOIL. BLESSINGS.` → `A FARMING BOOK THAT STARTS WITH THANKS.`

segments.voice: Why blessings come first. Start with what's inside Berakhot. It opens with the Shema, the words said at night and in the morning. Then the standing prayer. Then food: which blessing for the fruit of a tree, which for what grows from the ground, which for bread. Then it walks out of the house and into the world. On seeing lightning or hearing thunder, the Mishnah says, a person blesses the one whose strength and might fill the world. On mountains, seas and deserts, the one who makes the work of creation. And a harder line: a person is to bless over bad news just as over good. So the first tractate is about a habit: meeting what comes with words of acknowledgment. Why put it at the head of the order about farms? The Mishnah doesn't explain itself, so readers have offered answers. One runs like this: the order of seeds is about what you owe from your harvest, the corner, the tithes, the first fruits. Before you learn what you owe, you learn whose it was to begin with. A companion work to the Mishnah, the Tosefta, puts the principle plainly: a person shouldn't taste anything without first saying a blessing. Its reason is a line from the Psalms, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof." Thank before you take. In this way of seeing, the blessing isn't decoration on a meal. It's the first act of the harvest.
screen: `SHEMA, PRAYER, THEN FOOD.` · `LIGHTNING, MOUNTAINS, AND BAD NEWS TOO.` · `BEFORE WHAT YOU OWE, WHOSE IT WAS.` · `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.` · then, large: `THANKS BEFORE THE HARVEST.`

segments.voice: Set something you're about to eat or drink in front of you and don't touch it yet; just look at it, and let the small urge to reach for it wait. Let your attention widen the way Berakhot walks out of the house: the light in the room, a sound outside. Before the first bite, if you pray, say the blessing your tradition uses; if not, a plain thank you to whoever and whatever brought it.
Why blessings come first. The order of seeds opens with Berakhot, so that before you learn what you owe from a harvest, you thank for it. Today's word.
Your line: thanks before the harvest. Whose it was comes before what you owe. See you tomorrow.

1070.title: The corner of the field (Mishnah Peah)
1070.hook: how much to leave for the poor, and who may gather it
1070.howItsDone: Jewish law treats the corner of the field as the poor's by right; where farming laws are kept in the land of Israel, some farmers still leave peah, and Jewish teachers draw on these laws when describing giving that protects the dignity of the one who receives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why blessings come first: before you learn what you owe, you thank for it. Your line: thanks before the harvest. Today, the part of the harvest that isn't the farmer's.

The wheat is down across the whole field except one end. There, a strip of grain still stands, gold and untouched, as if the reapers forgot it. They didn't. The farmer's work is done, and he's gone home. Later, people who own no field at all come with their own sickles and cut it themselves. Nobody hands it to them. Nobody picks who gets some. It's theirs by right. The Torah asks for this strip, and the Mishnah gives it a whole tractate. How big? And who takes it?
screen: `ONE END OF THE FIELD STILL STANDING.` → `THEY CUT IT THEMSELVES.` → `HOW BIG? WHO TAKES IT?`

segments.voice: The corner of the field. In Hebrew, peah. The Torah's command, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corner of thy field." Leave it, it says, for the poor and for the stranger. It never says how much. So the Mishnah, in tractate Peah, asks. It admits the Torah set no measure, then sets a floor: no less than one sixtieth. The right amount depends on the size of the field, the number of the poor, and how good the harvest was. A floor, but no ceiling. A big year and a crowd of hungry people should mean a bigger corner. The second question: who gathers it? The Mishnah says the corner is given while the grain still stands, and the poor reap it themselves. The farmer doesn't cut it and hand it out to people he likes. There are exceptions, grapes on high trellises and dates at the top of tall palms, where the owner brings the fruit down and divides it. But the rule is that the corner isn't the farmer's gift. It belongs to the poor, and they come and take what is theirs. Near its close, the tractate turns to the one who takes. In paraphrase: whoever takes without needing to will not leave the world before coming to need others. And whoever truly needs, and holds back from taking, will live to support others from their own. The corner is for those who need it, and the one who takes is asked to be honest about that.
screen: `PEAH: THE TORAH GIVES NO SIZE.` · `NO LESS THAN A SIXTIETH; NO CEILING.` · `THE POOR REAP IT THEMSELVES.` · `TAKE ONLY IF YOU NEED.` · then, large: `THE CORNER.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you'll have plenty of today: food in the fridge, time, money, patience. Picture its corner, the part you could leave standing for someone else, without deciding who will get it, because that's the point of the corner. Then picture it set where someone who needs it can reach it without having to ask.
The corner of the field. Peah: the edge of the harvest left standing for the poor, at least a sixtieth, and reaped by the poor themselves. Today's word.
screen: `THE CORNER OF THE FIELD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the corner. It's theirs by right, not a favor. Go gently.

1071.title: Appointed times
1071.hook: the second order: Shabbat, festivals and fasts
1071.howItsDone: Jews keep a shared calendar of Shabbat, festivals and fasts, and the laws for each are studied in the tractates of the order Moed; today the Hebrew calendar is fixed by calculation rather than by witnesses to the new moon.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the corner of the field, left standing for the poor to reap. Your line: the corner. Today, the second order.

Two great sages disagree about when the new month began. It sounds small. It isn't. If the month began on a different day, then Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, falls on a different day too. Rabban Gamaliel, head of the court, has fixed the date. Rabbi Joshua is convinced he got it wrong. So Rabban Gamaliel sends an order: come to me with your walking staff and your money, on the day that by your count is Yom Kippur. On a fast day, you don't travel or carry money. He is asking Rabbi Joshua to break his own holy day in public. What will Rabbi Joshua do?
screen: `WHEN DID THE MONTH BEGIN?` → `COME WITH YOUR STAFF AND YOUR MONEY.` → `ON YOUR OWN YOM KIPPUR.`

segments.voice: Moed. Appointed time. The second of the six orders is the order of holy time, with tractates named for the days themselves: Shabbat. Pesachim, for Passover. Yoma, the Day, meaning Yom Kippur. Sukkah. Rosh Hashanah. Taanit, on fasts. Megillah, on Purim. Over the coming days you'll open several of them. The name comes from the Torah's own words for the festivals. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "These are the appointed seasons of the LORD." And the verse goes on: holy gatherings, which ye shall proclaim. Back to Rabbi Joshua, in tractate Rosh Hashanah. He is deeply troubled. Rabbi Akiva comes to him with that same verse: the festivals are the ones you proclaim. Whether the court sets the date at the right time or not, these are the appointed seasons. Another sage adds: if we question every court's ruling, there will be no end to it. So Rabbi Joshua takes his staff and his money and walks to Rabban Gamaliel on the day he himself believed was Yom Kippur. Rabban Gamaliel stands up, kisses him on the head, and says, in paraphrase: come in peace, my teacher and my student. My teacher in wisdom, my student because you accepted my word. That's what this order is about. Holy time has rules, and the rules are kept together: a calendar a whole people keeps as one.
screen: `MOED: THE ORDER OF HOLY TIME.` · `THE APPOINTED SEASONS, WHICH YE PROCLAIM.` · `RABBI JOSHUA TAKES UP HIS STAFF.` · `MY TEACHER AND MY STUDENT.` · then, large: `HOLY TIME HAS RULES.`

segments.voice: Picture the month ahead and look for the times already appointed: a Shabbat, a holiday, a birthday, the anniversary of a loss, a standing dinner with someone you love. Notice which ones you protect and which get pushed around, and choose one to keep with the steadiness a community keeps its calendar. If you keep Shabbat or the festivals, you might look at how this month's fall.
